paragraphs: The following assessments concern routine machinery maintenance by machinery maintenance workers. They do not predict hiring, qualifications, authorization, or contract outcomes.

The core work of machinery maintenance workers is to lubricate and routinely maintain production machinery under procedures to keep it running: read work orders and specifications to identify maintenance targets, lubricate or apply materials under specified procedures, dismantle and remove parts, inspect, test, and mark defects, install replacement parts and attachments to specifications, reassemble after repairs, start machines and observe operation to assess efficiency and problems, clean machines and parts and remove hardened material, replace linings and fluids, prepare and test chemical solutions for cleaning or repair, troubleshoot electrical, hydraulic, and mechanical faults, record production and repair information, and inventory and request parts.

Entirely fictional task package: provide a fictional equipment maintenance work order, including 1 machine requiring maintenance, 1 lubrication and spare part list, and 1 operational abnormality. Within 60 minutes, write maintenance sequences, lubrication and replacement points, abnormality judgments and shutdown conditions, and documentation and reporting steps. Do not use real company, equipment, or product data.

Sample output and reflection: check whether you first verified work orders and safety conditions, lubricated and replaced parts under procedures, specified abnormality judgments and shutdown conditions, and provided documentation and reporting paths. Then ask whether you can remain attentive during repetitive maintenance and downtime pressure, and whether you are willing to take responsibility for equipment operation and safety.

This page covers O*NET 49-9043.00 machinery maintenance workers: lubricating machinery, changing parts, or performing other routine machinery maintenance. Work includes reading orders and specifications, lubrication or material application, dismantling and removing parts, inspecting, testing, and marking defects, installing replacement parts and attachments, reassembling after repairs, starting and observing operation, cleaning and replacing linings, preparing chemical solutions, troubleshooting electrical, hydraulic, and mechanical faults, documenting, and requesting supplies. Work mainly involves machinery maintenance on production sites. This page excludes adjacent roles such as industrial machinery mechanics, millwrights, and general maintenance and repair workers.

entries: Inputs: production machinery and parts requiring maintenance, work orders and specifications, lubricants and adhesives, hand tools and lifting equipment such as chain hoists, jacks, and cranes, cleaning solvents and chemical solutions, spare parts and lining materials, and maintenance and production record forms.

Inspectable outputs: lubricated and routinely maintained machinery, correctly replaced and reassembled parts and attachments, inspection, testing, and defect marking records, operational observations and abnormality records, cleaning and lining replacement results, part and supply request records, and maintenance information records.

Complete workflow: read work orders and specifications to identify targets → check safety and shutdown conditions → lubricate, apply materials, and maintain under procedures → dismantle, inspect, test, and mark defects → replace parts and attachments and reassemble → start, observe operation, and assess problems → clean, replace linings and fluids, document, and request supplies.

paragraphs: Key judgments: whether maintenance intervals and lubrication requirements are met, whether defective parts should be replaced or repaired, when operational abnormalities require shutdown and reporting, whether cleaning and chemical solution use are safe, and which faults exceed this role's authorization and require specialist trades.

Environment and pace: mainly production sites, mostly full time, involving standing, bending, handling items, and using tools and lifting equipment. Hazardous equipment, noise, and chemicals may be present. Accuracy and safety requirements are high, with time pressure from production pace and downtime.

Research inputs: occupational identity, tasks, work activities, work context, skills and knowledge, interest code, education, and Job Zone for O*NET 49-9043.00. Pay, employment, and industry data on that page cover this occupation. These findings do not establish mainland Chinese qualifications, wages, or employment categories.

Check first: work orders and maintenance specifications, shutdown and energy isolation conditions, lubrication and part requirements, tool and lifting equipment condition, chemical solution and protection requirements, and boundaries for handing over work beyond authorization.

Work cycle: begin with orders and specifications, continue through safety and shutdown checks, lubrication and maintenance, dismantling, inspection and testing, replacement and reassembly, and startup observation, and finish with cleaning, replacement, documentation, and supply requests. Do not dismantle before shutdown and safety conditions are confirmed or deliver equipment before operational abnormalities are handled.

Boundaries with adjacent duties: this page covers only machinery maintenance workers. Industrial machinery mechanics perform in-depth diagnosis and repair, millwrights assemble equipment, and general maintenance and repair workers cover equipment and building maintenance across trades. In-depth diagnosis and work across systems must not be treated as interchangeable with this role.

Industrial machinery mechanics perform in-depth diagnosis and repair of industrial machinery, often involving control systems. Machinery maintenance workers focus on lubrication, part replacement, and routine maintenance, often handing over in-depth diagnosis.
Millwrights install and align equipment. Machinery maintenance workers maintain operating equipment and replace parts; installation and alignment form only part of their tasks.

General maintenance and repair workers cover equipment and building maintenance across trades. Machinery maintenance workers focus on lubrication and routine maintenance of production machinery; work scope and specialization differ.
Machinists produce precision parts from drawings. Machinery maintenance workers maintain and replace machine parts; part manufacture is often referred to machinists or machining roles.

The latter may organize fictional lubrication / maintenance record drafts; no adoption rates or job outcomes were obtained for this occupation. Automated text cannot replace on-site inspections or machinery repair authorization. AI Impact Score 8% is an editorial estimate. Occupational sources describe actual tasks and objects handled: machinery and parts, orders and specifications, tools and chemicals, and maintenance and operation records. Tool capabilities, organizational adoption, and job outcomes are recorded separately; pay or employment data do not substitute for AI evidence.

Editorial analysis: lubrication plans, monitoring alerts, and record summaries may be trial candidates. No comparison of AI automation levels across stages was obtained for this occupation. Traditional condition monitoring and CMMS are also not generative AI; on-site maintenance remains subject to procedures and authorization.

Human control points include checking work orders and shutdown conditions, lubricating and replacing parts under procedures, inspecting and marking defects, judging operational abnormalities and deciding on handover, and taking responsibility for equipment operation and safety.

Start with an offline exercise using an entirely fictional equipment maintenance order. Record maintenance sequences, lubrication and replacement, and abnormality judgment boundaries, without relying on unverified automated monitoring to replace human confirmation.

Editorial trial suggestion: a small sample draft using fictional materials only. Ordinary dedicated software differs from generative AI; widespread organizational adoption in this occupation has not been established.
Follow work orders and shutdown and safety procedures, retaining human inspections and records.

Fit signals: start with observable work behavior

To assess fit, first consider whether you can patiently lubricate and perform routine maintenance under procedures, dismantle, inspect, and replace parts by hand, remain attentive under downtime and production pressure, follow shutdown and chemical safety procedures, and take responsibility for equipment operation and safety. Tools such as RIASEC can only suggest hypotheses and cannot replace real task experience.
Positive signals: attentive maintenance under procedures, hands-on dismantling and part replacement, compliance with shutdown and chemical procedures, and documentation and collaboration.

Reasons for caution: difficulty with prolonged repetitive maintenance, a tendency to miss lubrication and inspection details, reluctance to follow shutdown and chemical protection procedures, or inability to judge whether faults exceed authorization.

Trial activity: use an entirely fictional equipment maintenance work order to practice maintenance sequencing, lubrication and replacement, inspection and defect marking, and operational judgments. Ask another person to review the records.

The RIASEC interest code is RC, Realistic–Conventional: a preference for hands-on maintenance under defined procedures. These labels describe activity preferences only and cannot determine competence or qualifications.

General personality scales such as the Big Five do not provide job evidence for this occupation and may be used only for self-reflection. Continue checking against real lubrication and maintenance, dismantling and inspection, and safe work experience.
Type tools such as MBTI and the Enneagram cannot determine competence or qualifications and may be used only for self-reflection.

Entry paths and stages of capability

US O*NET Job Zone3 is a general preparation group description, not evidence that most workers in this occupation need an associate degree or one to two years of training. Its education survey lists 54% postsecondary certificates, 41% high school, and 3% associate degrees. These are surveyed requirement distributions, not legal thresholds. BLS describes preparation as typically high school and on-the-job training; its training duration passages are inconsistent, so no fixed timeline is promised.

US BLS separates machinery maintenance on-the-job learning from millwright apprenticeship paths. Millwright apprenticeship proportions cannot establish that apprenticeships are common in this occupation. No precise Chinese qualification mapping has been established. Check tasks, equipment, jurisdiction, and employer authorization, with separate checks for specialist work such as electrical tasks.

Training certificates, occupational qualifications, and specialist licenses such as electrical licenses are different statuses. Certification does not automatically confer specialist work authority or licensure. Obtain relevant qualifications under local jurisdiction and employer authorization requirements.

Entry stage: practice lubrication and routine maintenance, tool and lifting equipment use, dismantling and inspection, and documentation under supervision. Learn shutdown and safety procedures and retain process records.

Evidence to show: provide a reviewable explanation of maintenance records, including orders, lubrication and replacement, inspection and defect marking, and operational judgments, to demonstrate maintenance under procedures and truthful documentation.

Next step: check the target employer's machinery types, shutdown and safety procedures, lubrication and part requirements, and authorization and handover boundaries. Validate inspection and safety skills through supervised real maintenance.

Moving toward greater responsibility: with experience, workers may handle complex machinery maintenance and maintenance plans, mentor new workers, or move into industrial machinery repair, condition monitoring, and equipment management.
Market signals and transition directions

Retained historical version: about 57,500 workers in 2024, decline during 2024–2034, and about 4,800 annual openings, which must not be described as a ten-year total. This is not the latest full-page version and does not establish individual hiring outcomes.
The page lists Manufacturing as the main industry in 2024. Employment and openings are statistical projections and must be explained separately from individual opportunities.

Transferable capabilities: lubrication and routine maintenance, dismantling and part replacement, inspection and testing and defect marking, tool and lifting equipment use, shutdown and chemical safety, and maintenance records.

Moving into industrial machinery repair requires complex industrial machinery fault diagnosis, control and hydraulic foundations, repair plans, testing and acceptance, and hazardous energy control. Routine lubrication and replacement experience does not establish competence in in-depth diagnosis and repair.

risks.mitigation: Trained, authorized personnel must isolate hazardous energy, control stored energy, and confirm a safe state under applicable equipment procedures. Do not dismantle before confirmation. A stop button does not equal energy isolation.
risks.scenario: Dismantling without shutdown or energy isolation.

risks.consequence: May cause crush injuries or strains.
risks.mitigation: Use lifting equipment and operate it correctly.
risks.scenario: Improper lifting equipment use or handling movements.

risks.mitigation: Check product labels and safety data sheets first. Use suitable protection and ventilation under equipment / chemical procedures and training. Stop and report unknown ingredients or conditions.
risks.scenario: Lubricant or chemical solution contact with skin or inhalation.

risks.consequence: May cause equipment damage or downtime.
risks.mitigation: Inspect, test, and review under procedures.

risks.mitigation: Clarify authorization boundaries and hand over promptly.

source_card.note: Check source scope, limitations, and statistical periods separately against original evidence. Source usage notes: O*NET 49-9043.00 Machinery Maintenance Workers (Summary) provides occupational identity, official description, interest code, Job Zone, skills, and knowledge for 49-9043.00. Pay and employment data on that page cover this occupation. O*NET 49-9043.00 Tasks provides tasks including lubrication and material application, dismantling and inspection, part replacement and reassembly, operational observation, cleaning and lining replacement, chemical solution preparation, troubleshooting, and records. The task sample does not imply that every job performs all tasks. O*NET 49-9043.00 Work Context describes production site work, standing and bending, tool and lifting equipment use, and hazardous equipment and noise exposure. US work context does not replace Chinese law or employer procedures. O*NET 49-9043.00 National Wages (BLS OEWS display) provides 2025 BLS OEWS median pay for this occupation. This page does not display pay percentiles. O*NET 49-9043.00 National Employment Trends provides 2024 employment and projections for growth and openings during 2024–2034. Projections do not guarantee hiring. Industries: 49-9043.00 lists Manufacturing as the main industry in 2024. Industry distribution signals employer settings, not projected growth or demand. O*NET 49-9043.00 Education and Job Preparation: Job Zone 3, most jobs require vocational school training, related experience or an associate degree, plus one to two years of training. The education distribution does not establish a mandatory requirement for every employer. National Certifications: 49-9043.00 is the US national certification lookup provided by O*NET. Certification and training do not establish specialist qualifications or employer hiring requirements. Generative AI and Jobs (ILO Working Paper 140, 2025) assesses occupational exposure to generative AI at the task level. The exposure index does not equal adoption rates, job outcomes, or hiring probabilities. Average Annual Wages of Employees in Urban Units in 2025 provides average annual wages by industry category for urban nonprivate and private units, including manufacturing. Industry averages are not occupational medians and exclude individual businesses and freelancers. Enterprise Remuneration Survey Information (2024) from the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security is a pay lookup organized by occupation / position. It covers urban enterprises, excluding government agencies and public institutions; this page did not obtain an entry precisely matching this occupation. The FermatMind Task Impact Scale for Machinery Maintenance Workers organizes tasks that tools may assist and human control points for task-level AI and fit discussion. The editorial scale is not evidence of adoption rates, layoffs, regulations, or credentials.

description.text: This page covers O*NET 49-9043.00 machinery maintenance workers: lubricating and routinely maintaining production machinery under procedures, dismantling and replacing parts and attachments, reassembling after repairs, inspecting, testing, and marking defects, starting and observing operation, cleaning and replacing linings, preparing chemical solutions, and recording maintenance information. To assess this career path, verify the work cycle, safety and authorization boundaries, evidence scope, risk controls, and observable beginner work samples together.

title.text: Assessing Machinery Maintenance Workers: Work, Entry Paths, and Risk Boundaries

subject.name: Machinery Maintenance Worker
subject.summary: This page covers O*NET 49-9043.00 machinery maintenance workers: lubricating machinery, changing parts, or performing other routine machinery maintenance, including dismantling and reassembly, inspection, testing and defect marking, starting and observing operation, troubleshooting electrical, hydraulic, and mechanical faults, and recording maintenance information.
